procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court of Rajasthan dated 19 October 2024 dismissing a Writ Petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Writ Petition was filed in the High Court of Rajasthan under Article 226 of the Constitution, raising identical issues to those brought before the Supreme Court. The High Court dismissed this petition on 19 October 2024.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via a Writ Petition (C) No. 708 of 2024 under Article 32 of the Constitution by 109 Petitioners. A petition for special leave was also preferred against the order of the High Court of Rajasthan. The Petitioners sought the quashing of the results of the main exams and re-evaluation of the answer sheets by an expert committee. The Supreme Court dismissed the petitions.

directions: Liberty given to candidates having individual grievances, except for issue concluded by this order, to move the High Court under Article 226.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was any arbitrary variation, deliberate low marking, or statistical discrepancy in the evaluation of the English Essay paper that would affect the integrity of the examination results and warrant the intervention of the Supreme Court under Article 32 for re-evaluation.

facts: Petitioners who took the Rajasthan Civil Judge Cadre main examination failed to qualify for the interview stage after receiving very low marks (between 0 and 15 out of 50) in the English Essay paper.
They alleged that the marking was skewed and unreasonably low, especially since there was no minimum qualifying score for the language paper.
A very high percentage of candidates (95.76%) scored within this low 0-15 mark range in the English Essay.
The petitioners filed a writ petition under Article 32 asking the Supreme Court to quash the results and order a re-evaluation of the answer sheets.
law: The Supreme Court can intervene in examination results under Article 32 of the Constitution if there is evidence of arbitrary variation, deliberate low marking, or a significant statistical discrepancy that affects the integrity of the exam.
If there is no significant variation in the strictness of evaluation between candidates who passed and those who failed, the marking process itself is not considered suspect.
application: To investigate the allegations, the Court ordered the production of the English Essay answer sheets for all candidates who scored below fifteen marks.

The judges personally perused these answer sheets and concluded that there was "no substance, even prima facie, in the allegations that there was a deliberate low marking." They found the low marks were justified by the quality of the answers.
The Court analyzed the statistical data, including the high percentage of low scores, but found "no statistical discrepancy that would warrant the intervention of this Court."

It also determined there was no "marked difference in the strictness of evaluation" for candidates who qualified for the interview versus those who did not, meaning the standard was applied consistently.
Ultimately, the Court found that the marking process did not suffer from any infirmity that would cast doubt on the overall assessment and integrity of the examination.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' claims, finding no evidence of arbitrary variation, deliberate low marking, or a statistical discrepancy in the evaluation of the English Essay paper. The petitions were dismissed, and no re-evaluation was ordered.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was any arbitrary variation, deliberate low marking, or statistical discrepancy in the evaluation of the English Essay paper that would affect the integrity of the examination results and warrant the intervention of the Supreme Court under Article 32 for re-evaluation.
appellant_arguments: There are serious discrepancies in the marks awarded to candidates for the English Essay examination.
Petitioners' marks in the English Essay paper were 'fatally low', ranging between zero and fifteen out of fifty.
The low marks warrant a re-evaluation of the answer papers by an expert committee and the setting aside of the examination results.
respondent_arguments: The evaluation process was designed to be fair, with the first question assessed by a District Judge level officer and the other two questions assessed by distinct sets of English Professors from a Government College.
The marks awarded were a true reflection of the candidates' performance, as evidenced by the answer sheets themselves.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will not intervene under Article 32 of the Constitution in the assessment of examination answer sheets where there is no statistical discrepancy or infirmity that would cast doubt on the overall assessment process.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: After personally perusing the answer sheets, the Court found no substance, even prima facie, to the allegations of deliberate low marking in the English Essay paper. Furthermore, an analysis of the tabulated results revealed no statistical discrepancy that would justify the Court's intervention under Article 32 of the Constitution, as the marking did not suffer from an infirmity that would cast doubt on the overall assessment process.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a statistical discrepancy exists that would warrant the intervention of the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution.
Whether the marking of an exam paper suffers from an infirmity that would cast doubt on the overall assessment.
Whether the petitions qualify the parameters for judicial intervention in examination results as established by a consistent line of precedent.
why_appellant_lost: The Court's direct perusal of the answer sheets revealed that there was no substance to the allegations of deliberate low marking, stating, 'Based on the nature of the answers in the English Essay, we have no doubt that there is no substance, even prima facie, in the allegations that there was a deliberate low marking in the English Essay paper.'

The Court found no statistical evidence to support the petitioners' claims, concluding, 'we find no statistical discrepancy that would warrant the intervention of this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution.'

The Court determined that the evaluation process was not fundamentally flawed, noting, 'The marking of the essay does not suffer from an infirmity that would cast doubt on the overall assessment of the English Essay answer sheets.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the marks were a true reflection of performance was validated by the Court's own examination of the answer sheets.
The Court's finding of no statistical discrepancy affirmed the integrity of the evaluation process which the respondent had defended.
policy_considerations: In the interest of justice and fairness, the Court took the step of directly scrutinizing the answer sheets to ensure the integrity of the examination process.

The Court maintained the distinction between its jurisdiction under Article 32 for systemic issues and the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 226 for individual grievances, granting liberty for the latter while dismissing the broader challenge.
